Surface rupture is one geologic hazard for which there are presently minimal structural solutions. In most cases buildings cannot withstand the ground displacement accompanying ground rupture. The Alquist-Priolo Geologic Hazard Zones Act of 1972 requires that no building for human occupancy be constructed within 50 feet of an active fault unless it can be proven that the development is not underlain by an active fault trace. Since the only fault directly affecting structures in CNRA's is classified as potentially active, (Silver Creek Fault), this state law does not apply.
Landslides:
Because all the areas included in the Community Development Block Grant program are in the valley floor, there is no landslide danger.
Liquefaction and Ground Failure:
Liquefaction and subsequent ground failure is a common phenomenon during major earthquakes. It can cause vertical distortions at the grounds furface, resulting in severe damage to structures because of settlement, tilting or floating. Lateral spreading, earth lurching, and differential settlement are other forms of ground failure associated with liquefaction.
The city-wide geotechnical investigation performed by Cooper-Clark Associates in 1974 distinguished five zones in San Jose of potential seismic-induced ground failure. These zones are mapped and give some indication of where seismically induced ground failures are most likely to occur rather than where there is a definite potential for such failures to occur. All of the above neighborhoods except Campus and Alma have creek banks, along which the lateral spreading hazard is especially high. The hazards associated with liquefaction in Alviso are a special concern. Liquefaction of the highly sensitive bay muds could cause vertical and lateral displacement of old and poorly engineered levees. Settlement of these structures would subject the community to severe saltwater flooding.
